correctness.rationale: The normalization gives \(\operatorname{tr}S=n\), and rank-one expansion gives \(\operatorname{tr}(S^2)=n+\sum_{j\ne k}a_{jk}a_{kj}\). For nonnegative eigenvalues, Cauchy gives \(n^2/d\le\operatorname{tr}(S^2)\). The triangle inequality and definition of \(M\) give \(n^2/d-n\le\sum_{j\ne k}|a_{jk}a_{kj}|\le n(n-1)M^2\). At the Welch value the endpoints coincide, so equality holds throughout. Equal eigenvalues plus diagonalizability gives \(S=(n/d)I\). Every one of the \(n(n-1)\) nonnegative summands must equal \(M^2\), and since each factor has modulus at most \(M\), both factors equal \(M\); the \(n=d\) case has \(M=0\). A fresh symbolic check verified the endpoint identity \(n(n-1)\gamma^2=n^2/d-n\).
